title: Google Antigravity MCP: How to Add Servers (2026)
summary: Google Antigravity MCP connects your IDE to external tools through MCP servers. You'll understand which servers expose data and functions to your agent.
body_markdown:
## Connect business workflows with Activepieces


Only when the agent has to touch business apps does[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/mcp) earn a place, with 750 integrations in an MIT-licensed core to reach them.


Activepieces lets you publish workflows as an MCP server that Antigravity connects to, and MCP access is included on the Free plan, which also carries unlimited flows and 1,000 credits a month, while the credentials stay in the platform, not in your IDE config.


That matters after the injection warning above: **a fetched page can steer the agent** , and the less the agent holds, the less a hijacked session can spend.


### When to add a workflow MCP server


If you only use Antigravity for coding, skip it. A repository server and a docs server cover that job, and a workflow layer is one more moving part to audit.


It starts to pay when the agent needs to reach a CRM, a ticketing queue, a spreadsheet or a mail tool. Otherwise you'd paste a separate token into each direct server.


Once a integration is connected in Activepieces, the agent can call it.


The same integration action runs as a step in a flow and as a tool schema on the per-project MCP server that Antigravity's server entry points at, so there is no second catalogue to publish to and no export step before the agent can use it.


Of the 750 integrations in the MIT-licensed open source repo, **roughly 60% are community-contributed** , and the code under packages/integrations/community is where you can confirm that the action a flow runs is the one the agent calls.


Because each workflow you expose is a fixed set of steps with the field mappings already decided, the agent calls the workflow and doesn't improvise against a raw API. That narrows what a bad instruction can do, which is the whole argument for starting narrow.


Be skeptical of catalogue counts, though. A long list of connectors says nothing about whether the trigger or action you need exists, or whether it exposes the field you need to map. Open the specific integration and read its actions before you commit.


The table compares the two routes on the three things that decide the choice. Read it as a trade: the workflow route centralises secrets and logging at the cost of building each workflow, while direct servers are quicker to wire but scatter both.


Activepieces workflows as an MCP server Direct vendor MCP servers


Where credentials live In the Activepieces platform's connections In each server's config or auth flow on your machine


Breadth of business apps 750 integrations, but only the apps you build workflows for Only vendors that ship their own server


Audit trail Run history in one place, per workflow Whatever each vendor logs, in separate places


What follows is how this looks from inside Antigravity.


### How the connection looks from Antigravity


From Antigravity's side, Activepieces, which MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run in production, is just another MCP server entry. You add the server address and its authentication the same way as any other, and the exposed workflows appear as tools. Nothing about the agent changes.


Confirm the exact steps for adding a custom server in Google's Antigravity documentation and in the Activepieces MCP Server documentation, since both interfaces change; the 2026-11-16 check date above applies to this section too.


Start with one read-only workflow, such as looking up a record. Run it, then check the run history on the Activepieces side to confirm the inputs match what you expected.


A run counts as 1 credit however many steps it has (AI steps cost more), so the test barely touches the Free plan's 1,000 credits a month.


Add write actions only after that check passes, and keep each one a separate workflow so you can switch it off alone.
